text.p: These are leading stories in this morning's Paris newspapers.
LES ECHOS
-- Prime Minister Alain Juppe drops practice of setting pay ceilings for companies in the public sector, firms will have to negotiate wage settlements individually with ministries.
-- EDF and GDF electricity and gas utilities sign agreement introducing a 32-hour week, designed to favour new hirings.

-- Credit Foncier workers hold chairman at Paris headquarters to protest planned partial transfer of activity to Credit Immobilier de France. Government named a mediator yesterday to defuse the crisis.
LA TRIBUNE
-- Finance Minister Jean Arthuis announces plans to cut interest rates on popular housing savings schemes, to bring them in line with other bank lending rates.
-- Survey shows 58 percent of traders believe Paris bourse has scope to rise, expect further rate cuts.

-- Prospects of monetary union fuel tensions between French and German authorities, Bundesbank governor worried by idea of a political counterweight to the future European monetary authority, called for by the French.
-- Eurotunnel to battle for 50 percent of cross-Channel traffic.
-- SNCF railroad operator expects a 2.9 percent rise in traffic volume through the year 2000.
L'AGEFI
-- Credit Agricole tops ranking for custodian for shareholders.
LE FIGARO-ECONOMIE
-- GDF utility chairman Pierre Gadonneix rules out extending widely a planned 32-hour work week, as it conceived as a voluntary measure.
-- Former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing pleased to see dollar reaching 5.5 francs, calls for further French rate cuts.
LIBERATION (Economic section)
-- President Jacques Chirac launches reform of the French justice system.
-- Eurotunnel calls for an extension of its debt standstill.
THE INTERNATIONAL HERALD TRIBUNE

-- Future president of European Monetary Institute Wim Duisenberg does not forecast major improvements on employment in Europe before the year 2000. The question of a political counterwieght to the future European central bank was raised six years ago and lost by the French, who nevertheless continue pushing the issue.
